There's less than one month ago before the 2026 midterm elections, and NPR's Domenico
Montanaro reports the political landscape appears to be changing more in favor of Democrats.
History isn't kind to the president's party in midterm elections, and this year is shaping
up to be no different.
Negative views of the economy and the Iran war have created a tough environment for swing
district Republicans.
Democrats are the favorites to pick up control of the House, and the Senate appears to be
within reach.
That isn't something that was thought possible at the beginning of the cycle.
But while Democrats are in the driver's seat, there are lots of reasons for why their gains
may be limited.
Redistricting has helped insulate Republicans to an extent.
Most of the districts that are competitive are in places Trump won in 2024, and the Democratic
Party remains unpopular.
Domenico Montanaro, NPR News, Washington.
The Justice Department is moving hundreds of detainees who are awaiting trial near Atlanta
to a detention center several hours away.
Legal groups and Democratic lawmakers say the transfer unlawfully cuts people off from
their lawyers, and that's not all.
NPR's Kristin Wright reports.
Attorneys for the detainees say the U.S. Marshals Service's decision to move their clients
almost 200 miles to a detention center in South Georgia separates them from family and
is a violation of their constitutional right to legal counsel.
The detainees are all facing federal criminal cases.
The Marshals Service plans to transfer about 400 people by the end of the month, according
to the non-profit federal defender program.
It tells NPR 20 to 30 of its clients have already been moved.
The group's executive director says attorneys traveling six hours round-trip and meeting
by video with clients would restrict their right to counsel and estimates it'll cost
taxpayers.
Georgia Public Broadcasting reports the Marshals Service set in a statement the decisions based
on "diverse challenges to ensure safe and secure confinement."
Kristin Wright, NPR News.
Most Israeli settlers have carried out multiple attacks against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied
West Bank in recent days.
The increase in attacks coincides with the start of the olive harvesting season.
Here's NPR's Kat Lonsdorf.
Israeli settlers burned dozens of olive trees owned by a Palestinian family south of East
Jerusalem on Saturday, according to local officials.
The day before, in separate incidents, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers near
Indianapolis, while masked settlers carrying bats also attacked a group of Israeli human-rights
activists trying to protect Palestinians as they harvested olives near Bethlehem.
The United Nations has documented significant spikes in settler attacks in the West Bank
during olive harvesting season in recent years, with an overall rise year over year in general.
Israel says it condemns such attacks, but there are usually few consequences for the
Israelis who carry them out.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Two people have been killed dozens injured during a block party in southern Georgia.
You're listening to NPR News.
The Coast Guard says it is still trying to account for the six people who were aboard
a medical plane that crashed off Nantucket early yesterday.
The jet was traveling from Bermuda to Boston when it lost contact with air traffic control.
Paul Canerney from member station WBUR in Boston has more.
The Coast Guard is located jet debris 20 miles off Nantucket, where Admiral Matt Lake describes
the search as a rescue operation, but did say they would continue to update the "next
of kin" as the operation unfolds.
This is a large and demanding search area.
Our crews are employing fixed-wing aircraft, helicopter, boats and cutters to search the
area and will continue to evaluate all available information as our operation progresses.
Lake said they are working with Massachusetts officials to dispatch crafts equipped with
sonar to scan the ocean floor.
The Coast Guard says they plan to search until they are confident they will not find any survivors.
For NPR News, I'm Paul Canerney in Boston.
The White House exhibit that has just gotten a new makeover called The People's House,
adjacent to the White House, has overhauled its replica of the Oval Office and now looks
like President Trump's Oval Office, complete with gold accents, included gilded frames,
trophies and other knickknacks.
There's also a copy of the Declaration of Independence, just like in the President's
actual office.
The exhibit is the same size as the real Oval Office, and visitors are often startled to
see about how small it really is.
The White House Historical Association created this Oval Office exhibit.
I'm Lyndi Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
